Growing Prosperity from the Ground Up Oil palm is a long-duration crop. Its successful expansion depends on farmer confidence, reliable procurement and consistent support throughout the cultivation cycle. We work with State Horticulture Departments, Government agencies, agricultural universities and research institutions to help farmers understand the crop, access eligible subsidies and adopt scientific practices. Our collaboration with the ICAR-Indian Institute of Oil Palm Research supports work on the early detection and management of pests and diseases.

Government assistance under the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil Palm helps lower the initial investment required from farmers. Support covers planting material, maintenance during the early years, intercropping, drip irrigation, water infrastructure and farm equipment. Our teams assist with awareness, documentation and coordination with the relevant authorities. During FY 2025-26, we expanded our oil palm network by adding 16,664 farmers and increased the area under cultivation to 1,10,722 hectares. We also strengthened on-ground infrastructure through additional collection centres and nurseries, particularly in the Northeast. These initiatives are helping improve farmer convenience, strengthen market access and build a more resilient domestic edible oils ecosystem.

SUPPORTING FARMERS ACROSS THE CULTIVATION CYCLE

Agronomy and training

Field teams advise farmers on nutrient management, irrigation, pest and disease management, harvesting and soil health. Customised fertiliser recommendations, supported by soil and leaf testing, help improve nutrient management and farm productivity.

Quality planting material

Nurseries provide healthy planting material suited to local cultivation conditions, supported by access to harvesting tools and other essential farm inputs.

Farmer awareness and onboarding

Village meetings, field demonstrations and oil palm drives introduce farmers to the crop and provide guidance on cultivation practices.

Technology and transparency

Geo-tagging of plantations supports area consolidation and improved crop management. Government-linked pricing, electronic weighment and digital records provide greater visibility across procurement, while direct online payments enable transparent and timely settlement with farmers.

Soil and water conservation

Bio-waste recycling and mulching help improve soil fertility and moisture retention while reducing water loss, supporting our focus on improving water-use efficiency and achieving ‘More Crop per Drop’.

Inputs and mechanisation

Palm Vikas Kendras provide fertilisers, crop protection products, tools, irrigation components and mulching material. We also promote mechanisation through equipment such as chaff cutters, sprayers and power weeders to address labour constraints and improve farm-level efficiency.

Timely market access

Decentralised procurement centres located close to plantation areas facilitate convenient access for farmers and timely procurement of Fresh Fruit Bunches.

Strengthening Farmer Collectives Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) enable individual cultivators to participate in organised agricultural value chains through collective procurement, aggregation, capacity building and market access. We support 202 FPOs across 12 States, including 100 in the Northeast and 102 across the rest of India.

During the year, we continued to provide operational guidance, training, procurement assistance and market linkage support to help FPOs develop as sustainable rural enterprises. We also supported access to quality agricultural inputs, farm machinery, digital services and modern cultivation practices.

Financial Risk Management We continue to adopt a proactive and structured approach to managing financial risks such as inflation, commodity-price movements and currency fluctuations. Our framework combines dynamic budgeting, vigilant market tracking and agile hedging strategies to protect liquidity, margins and investor confidence. The framework was tested in real time during FY 2025-26 as the edible oil complex witnessed renewed volatility following crude-oil price movements and geopolitical uncertainty. Between January and March 2026, RBD palm and deodorised palm oil prices increased by approximately 20%, while refined soya oil prices increased by approximately 23%. Cost of goods sold consequently increased by 98 basis points sequentially and 294 basis points year-on-year. We responded through calibrated pricing realignments, commodity and forex hedging, supplier negotiations and continued cost control. Our treasury team actively monitors commodity and currency markets, hedging exposures through approved policies and leveraging natural hedging where feasible.

Underlying Considerations

Removals over offsets

Carbon sequestered by a maturing oil palm plantation represents nature-based carbon removal, actively removing atmospheric carbon and storing it in its biomass. This provides a more direct and tangible climate approach than the emissions reductions claimed through externally purchased offset credits, which have faced emerging global scrutiny issues of additionality and permanence.

Alignment with India's national glide path

Our approach is consistent with India's commitment to achieve net zero by 2070, as announced in COP26. We are building credible, incremental milestones as part of our climate strategy through a phased, plant-level approach aligned with the national trajectory.

Two genuinely owned climate assets

Only a few companies within the edible oils or FMCG sector simultaneously operate a utility scale renewable energy portfolio and a large, mature and nature-based carbon sink. This combination allows Patanjali Foods to make near term and verifiable neutrality claims grounded within its own physical assets’ operations, rather than externally purchased carbon credits or offsets of variable quality.

Scope 3 data maturity

The visibility across value chain emissions, spanning agricultural raw materials, third-party logistics and purchased goods, is still being progressively built to establish a complete, auditable Scope 3 baseline for a credible net zero commitment. Committing to net zero ahead of this maturity would risk an unsubstantiated pledge rather than a verifiable one.

A staged foundation for net zero

Achieving carbon neutrality at individual plant-level provides an auditable and replicable template that can be extended across the Company's operational footprint, and over time, the wider value chain.

The Company has initiated tracking of its Scope 3 GHG emissions from FY 2025-26, covering Purchased Goods and Services, Business Travel, and Employee Commuting. Going forward, the Company intends to progressively expand its Scope 3 tracking to cover all applicable categories and strengthen its Scope 3 emissions assessment and disclosure practices.

Renewable energy is one of our key climate assets in our transition towards cleaner and more resilient energy sources across the manufacturing operations. Wind power remains a significant component of the portfolio, complemented by solar power and renewable-fuel-based energy generation through back-pressure turbines and boilers using biomass fuels such as husk and palm fibre. Together, these diversified sources enable us to generate and utilise renewable energy across operations, reduce dependence on conventional grid electricity and fossil fuels, improve energy security and support our broader climate strategy and long-term decarbonisation journey.

The Science Behind Unlike annual or seasonal crops, which store carbon and release it back into the atmosphere during harvest, oil palm is a long-lived perennial plantation that typically remains in production for 25 to 30 years. Across this growth cycle, the palm continuously accumulates biomass both above ground (trunk, fronds and canopies) and below ground (root systems). As the plantation matures, these living carbon sinks continue to capture and store atmospheric carbon, contributing to the Company's climate mitigation efforts through biological carbon sequestration, and complementing the emissions avoided through our renewable energy portfolio.

The rate of carbon accumulation is closely tied to the plantation's age profile. Biomass and carbon storage accrue most rapidly during the young-to-prime growth phase and broadly during the 4 th to 25 th year of a palm's life before tapering as the tree reaches full maturity.

Farmer Livelihoods and Sustainable Sourcing

Our approach to oil palm cultivation prioritises sustainability and socio-economic upliftment, with plantation development focussed on degraded, low-productivity agricultural land and wastelands while avoiding the conversion of forest areas. Grown predominantly as a smallholder crop, oil palm replaces seasonal produce without displacing natural biodiversity. Compared with several competing oilseed crops, oil palm requires relatively fewer fertilisers and pesticides – making it, on a per-hectare basis, a comparatively environmentally favourable source of edible oil. With careful land-use planning, our oil palm cultivation model is evolving into a genuinely climate-conscious agricultural practice, one that intentionally decouples plantation expansion from deforestation risk.

Responsible Land Use We are strengthening sustainability and mill-to plantation traceability in palm oil sourcing through satellite technology, geolocation, and artificial intelligence. Our iAgro Geo-Tag initiative maps plantations and captures periodic field data with images and videos, supported by regular audits and third-party verification. This digital traceability infrastructure is a critical enabler of credible deforestation-free claims at scale, particularly as the plantation network continues to expand into new states.

Our plantation network supports sustainable sourcing and livelihoods of the farmers who cultivate it, creating a model in which climate value, agricultural livelihoods, and supply chain resilience reinforce one another. Strengthening Farmer Livelihoods As of March 2026, we supported 80,579 farmer beneficiaries through our oil palm programme, with 238 farmer information and FFB procurement centres, 48 state-of-the-art nurseries, and 21 fertiliser godowns. Building a Traceable Supply Chain Digitisation initiatives including geo-tagging of plantations, RFID farmer identification, electronic weighing, and the iPalm procurement monitoring solution strengthen the traceability from farm to mill and improve transparency in farmer payments. The Company also continued to use technology-enabled traceability and plantation monitoring to strengthen the credibility and resilience of its growing natural carbon sink.

Regenerative Agriculture and Landscape Resilience The Company's plantation management practices are designed to support regenerative agriculture, healthy soils, and long-term landscape resilience. Farmers are supported in mulching with pruned fronds and organic matter, a practice that can increase soil carbon and nitrogen content. Intercropping and cover-cropping further improve soil fertility and moisture retention, strengthening the plantation's role as a durable natural carbon sink while supporting the broader ecosystems in which it operates.

A Zero-Waste, Circular Climate Value Chain The climate value of our oil palm network extends beyond the plantation to the mills that process the harvested fruit. It creates compounding climate benefits across the value chain – carbon sequestration during cultivation and use of processing by-products in displacing fossil energy once the fruit is harvested, enabling circular resource use. From Biomass to Energy Boilers fuelled by palm fibre (~13% of processed output) and shell (~4.5%) generate steam for electricity and heating requirements at our oil palm mills, reducing reliance on fossil fuels to fulfil for thermal and power needs.

Conservation of Energy, Technology Absorption, Foreign Exchange Earnings and Outgo [Pursuant to Section 134(3)(m) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 8(3) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014] The Company is committed to conducting its operations in a safe, responsible and environmentally sustainable manner, with a focus on energy conservation, resource efficiency, adoption of renewable energy, technological advancement and reduction of the environmental impact of its operations. As part of its sustainability and operational excellence initiatives, the Company continuously evaluates opportunities to improve energy efficiency, optimize utility consumption, enhance process performance, recover waste energy, increase the use of renewable and alternate energy sources, and adopt advanced technologies across its manufacturing facilities. During the year under review, the Company made significant investments in energy-efficient equipment, process optimization, heat recovery, utility optimization, energy monitoring and renewable energy initiatives. During financial year 2025–26, the Company completed energy conservation and sustainability-related capex of approximately ₹8.54 crore across its manufacturing locations. (A) Conservation of Energy (I) Steps taken to use Green and Renewable Energy

The Company continues to enhance the use of renewable and alternate energy sources as part of its long-term strategy to reduce dependence on conventional energy and minimize its carbon footprint.

• The Company generates approximately 60.85 MW of power from wind energy, of which approximately 17.35 MW is utilised for captive consumption. Power generated from wind projects located in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka is utilised at the Company’s manufacturing facilities at Nagpur, Kandla, Manglia, Chennai and Mangaluru, respectively. 
• The Company operates husk-fired boilers at selected manufacturing facilities, including Baran, Sriganganagar and Kakinada, facilitating the utilisation of biomass/agro residue as an alternate fuel and reducing dependence on conventional fossil fuels. 
• The Haldia and Kandla manufacturing facilities also utilise electricity generated through back-pressure and condensing turbine systems, thereby improving energy efficiency through cogeneration. A 4.2 MW back-pressure turbine is under commissioning at the Manglia Plant and is expected to be commissioned by the end of next year. 
• The Company operates a 500 KW Solar Power Plant at its Bhagwanpur facility for captive consumption, contributing to increased utilisation of renewable energy. 
• The Company has also proposed the replacement of its existing wind turbines. The proposal is presently under consideration by the Board of Directors. 

(II) Steps taken and impact on Conservation of Energy

The Company has undertaken various initiatives across its manufacturing facilities to improve energy efficiency, reduce energy intensity and optimize the consumption of utilities. Steam and Thermal Energy Conservation Key initiatives include:

• Regular monitoring and maintenance of steam traps to minimize avoidable steam losses. 
• Improved insulation of valves, bends, flanges and other hot surfaces to reduce thermal losses. 
• Recovery and reuse of condensate to improve steam system efficiency. 
• Optimization of open-steam usage in refinery and process operations. 
• Installation and upgradation of Plate Heat Exchangers (PHEs), heat recovery systems, economizers, air pre heaters and boiler heat-recovery systems to recover process and flue-gas heat. 
• Optimization of boiler combustion through online oxygen analysers, improved combustion controls and automation systems. 
• Installation and revamping of boiler systems, ESPs, coils, burners and associated equipment to improve boiler efficiency and reduce fuel consumption. 
• Installation of steam flow meters and other measurement systems for improved steam monitoring and energy management. 
• Optimization of turbine and vacuum systems to improve steam utilisation and minimize energy losses. 
• Installation of Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) for fans, pumps and other energy-intensive equipment to optimize power consumption according to process requirements. 
• Replacement of inefficient motors, pumps, compressors and other rotating equipment with high efficiency equipment. 
• Installation and upgradation of high-efficiency chillers, cooling towers and refrigeration systems. 
The Company has also undertaken comprehensive Steam 
Energy Audits through Forbes Marshall at manufacturing 
facilities including Kandla, Patalganga, Chennai, Mangaluru, 
Haldia, Kakinada, Nagpur and Washim. Recommendations 
arising from these audits have been progressively implemented 
to improve steam efficiency, reduce fuel and utility consumption 
and strengthen overall energy performance. 
Electrical Energy Conservation

• Improvement of compressed-air systems through energy efficient compressors, air dryers and associated controls. 
• Installation of efficient pumping systems and motors for water, cooling and process applications. 
• Installation and upgradation of PLC, SCADA and automation systems to improve process control and energy efficiency. 
• Installation of energy meters, ABT meters, steam flow meters and other monitoring systems to strengthen measurement, analysis and control of energy consumption. 
• Boiler efficiency and fuel-saving projects 
• Heat recovery and thermal energy optimization 
• High-efficiency pumps, motors and compressors 
• VFD-based electrical energy optimization

(III) Steps taken for utilisation of Alternate Sources of Energy

The Company continues to evaluate and adopt alternate sources of energy based on technical feasibility, operational requirements and commercial viability. The key focus areas include:

• Increased utilisation of renewable energy, including wind and solar power, for captive consumption. 
• Utilisation of biomass/Agro-residue, including husk, as an alternate boiler fuel at suitable locations. 
• Cogeneration through back-pressure and condensing turbine systems. 
• Refurbishment and performance enhancement of renewable energy assets. 
• Evaluation of additional renewable energy and energy efficient technologies to reduce dependence on conventional energy sources. 

(IV) Other Energy, Water and Environmental Sustainability Initiatives

The Company’s sustainability initiatives extend beyond energy conservation to include water conservation, waste reduction, emission control and efficient utilisation of natural resources. Key initiatives include:

• Installation and operation of Reject Recycle RO systems to improve water recovery and reduce water wastage. 
• Reuse of RO reject water and boiler blowdown water in cooling tower applications, wherever technically feasible. 
• Continued adoption of physical refining processes to optimize chemical and utility consumption. 
• Installation and operation of Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems at manufacturing facilities including Patalganga, Padartha, Ampapuram, Kakinada, Chennai, Mangaluru and Manglia, with systems under commissioning at Kandla and Nagpur. 
• Installation and operation of Online Continuous Monitoring Systems (OCMS/SPM) for continuous monitoring of emissions. 
• Installation and upgradation of Electrostatic Precipitators (ESPs) for effective control of particulate emissions, including the recent installation at Patalganga. 
• Operation of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) for treatment, recycling and reuse of wastewater. 
• Continuous improvement in water, energy and utility monitoring through digital measurement, automation and process-control systems. 

(V) Capital Investment on Energy Conservation Equipment

During financial year 2025–26, the Company completed energy conservation and sustainability-related Capex of approximately ₹8.54 crore. (B) Technology Absorption (I) Efforts made towards Technology Absorption

The Company continues to strengthen its manufacturing capabilities through the adoption and modernization of energy efficient technologies, process automation and advanced utility-management systems. The Company’s technical and manufacturing teams continuously evaluate new technologies and process improvements aimed at enhancing productivity, equipment reliability, resource utilization and environmental performance. During the year, the Company implemented and upgraded various technologies, including:

• Advanced PLC and SCADA-based automation and control systems 
• Online energy and process monitoring systems 

• High-efficiency boilers, burners, pumps, motors, compressors, chillers and cooling systems 
• Heat recovery systems, PHEs and air pre-heaters 
• Online oxygen analysers for boiler combustion optimization 
• VFD-based control systems for energy-intensive equipment 
• Advanced steam and utility metering systems 
• Energy-efficient refrigeration and cooling technologies 
• Improved water treatment, RO and utility recovery systems 
• Cogeneration and turbine-based power generation systems 
• Renewable energy and energy recovery solutions The Company also undertakes energy assessments, process studies, technical audits and equipment performance evaluations to identify opportunities for technology upgradation and optimization. 

(II) Benefits Derived from Technology Absorption

The adoption of advanced technologies and process improvements has enabled the Company to:

• Improve manufacturing and utility efficiency 
• Reduce energy and utility consumption and associated operating costs 
• Improve boiler, turbine, refrigeration, pumping and cooling-system efficiency 
• Recover and reuse process and thermal energy 
• Strengthen process control and operational reliability 
• Enhance equipment performance and plant productivity 
• Reduce fuel consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions 
• Improve water utilisation, recovery and recycling 
• Strengthen data-based energy monitoring and management 
• Improve environmental performance and reduce the Company’s carbon footprint 
• Enhance resource efficiency and long-term sustainability 
• Optimize the use of available technologies and support import substitution, wherever technically and commercially feasible The Company will continue to evaluate emerging technologies, automation solutions, renewable energy opportunities and other sustainability initiatives to enhance competitiveness and meet evolving environmental, operational and regulatory requirements. 

(III) Imported Technology

The Company has not imported any technology during the last three financial years, reckoned from the beginning of the financial year under review.

Commodity price risk or foreign exchange risk and hedging activities: In the normal course of business, the Company is exposed to risks relating to commodity price fluctuations, volatility in foreign currency exchange rates, and variations in interest rates. To address these risks, the Company has established Board approved Foreign Exchange Risk Management and Commodity Price Risk Management Policies, which lay down the principles and practices for risk mitigation.

The Company is exposed to Foreign Exchange Risk on account of transactions denominated in foreign currencies, primarily export sales and import purchases. In accordance with the Risk Management Policy, foreign currency exposures are hedged and the Company employs hedging instruments such as foreign exchange forward contracts and futures contracts to mitigate risks arising from foreign currency exposures. The Company is also subject to Commodity Price Risk from fluctuations in the prices of agricultural commodities and raw materials, particularly those sourced from overseas markets. To mitigate commodity price risks, the Company undertakes hedging strategies that include sale of futures contracts on domestic and international commodity exchanges, contracts of sale, and mutually agreed supply arrangements with suppliers. In line with policy, the Company restricts itself to plain vanilla derivative instruments, thereby maintaining a prudent approach to risk management. As part of a robust framework, a dedicated Risk Management Committee has been constituted by the Board, which meets periodically to review risk exposures, approve methodologies, and oversee the implementation and effectiveness of the Risk Management Policy and practices. As at 31 st March, 2026, the Company’s hedged commodity exposure stood at ` 102 crore (on estimated basis) which is in line with the risk management policy of the Company.

Management Discussion and Analysis

Global Economy The world economy maintained stability throughout 2025 by handling shifting trade rules and mixed results across regions. Heavy investments in technology offset the impact of fresh tariffs and changing government policies. Global inflation settled at a manageable 4.1% as many countries delivered numbers below what markets first predicted.

The geopolitical environment remains uncertain, with escalating tensions in West Asia emerging as a key risk for global trade, energy flows and supply chains. Recent developments in the region have increased concerns around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy shipments, while also contributing to higher crude oil prices, tighter LNG availability and broader market volatility. At the same time, the Russia-Ukraine conflict continues to affect oil supply, commodity prices and logistics, adding to the pressure on global markets. These developments are likely to create indirect challenges across sectors through higher input costs, shipment delays and uncertainty in the availability of essential materials and services.

Household spending increased steadily across the world in 2025, driven by tech spending and higher wages in major areas. Consumers in the United States and emerging Asian countries spent more on goods and services as financial conditions improved. This stronger demand helped soften the blow from tariff pressures. Global job markets were resilient in 2025 despite trade disruptions and policy uncertainty. Technology and services sectors added jobs steadily while manufacturing growth slowed. Reliable employment levels supported rising household incomes and broader economic strength.

World GDP expanded by 3.5% in 2025, showing varied speeds across regions. Advanced economies achieved 1.9% growth, with the United States reaching 2.1% through technology investments and policy backing. The euro area recorded 1.4% while Japan managed 1.1%. Emerging markets outperformed with 4.5% overall growth led by India's strong 7.7% expansion and China's steady 5.0% rise.

Trade tensions remained a key source of uncertainty during the period, as the legal status of US tariff actions and the future of related bilateral arrangements became less certain following the Supreme Court ruling that struck down the Trump tariffs. This development added to the unpredictability around future tariff rates, trade policy direction, and the durability of recent bilateral understandings.

Policy uncertainty remained elevated, even as businesses continued to adjust to the changing trade environment. Financial conditions stayed broadly supportive overall, while artificial intelligence-related investment and wider technology spending continued to provide an important offset to trade-related headwinds.

Central banks controlled inflation with measured adjustments, including interest rate cuts in the United States and the United Kingdom. These careful steps preserved financial stability amid ongoing trade frictions and political developments. (Source: World Economic Outlook (IMF))

Outlook The global economy moves toward steady growth projected at 3.0% for 2026 before easing slightly to 3.4% in 2027. Technology-led productivity gains, particularly from artificial intelligence spreading into industry and medicine, drive this progress. These advances help offset ongoing trade tensions and shifting political landscapes.

Advanced economies should expand by 1.7% in 2026. The United States leads this group with expected 2.3% growth supported by tax incentives under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Market recovery after the short 2025 federal shutdown creates ideal conditions for private investment and consumer spending. The euro area moderates at 0.9%, serving as a reliable global anchor. Japan recalibrates to 0.6% growth following recent policy adjustments.

Emerging markets maintain strong momentum at 3.8% growth. China projects 4.6% expansion in 2026 backed by domestic stimulus and improved US trade relations. India continues as a leading performer with 6.4% growth, positioning as a global hub for manufacturing and digital transformation.

Global headline inflation increases gradually to 4.7% in 2026 and further declines to 3.9% in 2027. Advanced economies approach inflation targets more slowly, particularly in the United States. Central banks adjust policy rates carefully, with gradual cuts in the United States and the United Kingdom, steady rates in the euro area and modest increases in Japan. World trade growth moderates to 3.5% in 2026 due to tariff adjustments, though technology exports continue providing essential support. (Source: World Economic Outlook (IMF))

India continues to remain one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies, supported by resilient domestic demand, strong investment activity, and ongoing structural reforms. However, the latest GDP estimates indicate that India is currently the 6 th largest economy in the world with a nominal GDP of about $4.15 trillion in 2026, and not the 4 th largest as previously stated after defeating Japan earlier. The country is expected to retain its strong growth momentum and may regain a higher global ranking over the medium term as economic expansion continues.

Private consumption remains a primary driver, aided by lower inflation and higher real incomes. Investments increased with public capital expenditure of ₹12.2 lakh crore (as per the Union Budget 2026-27), which enhanced infrastructure and spurred activity in manufacturing, construction, and energy. Government initiatives like Viksit Bharat 2047 promote self-reliance and capacity building despite external pressures.

Average headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) Inflation (retail inflation) reached a historic low of 1.7% during the first nine months of FY 2025-26. This price stability has been a key driver in strengthening domestic purchasing power. However, the inflation rate has risen to 3.4%, mostly due to challenges stemming from the West Asian conflicts. This stability is supported by disciplined government spending and steady growth in bank credit. Furthermore, the banking sector remains resilient with strong capital reserves and low levels of bad loans. With foreign exchange reserves exceeding $700 billion, India has become the fourth-largest economy and is well-positioned to withstand global volatility.

(Source: PIB)

Outlook The outlook for the Indian economy remains positive and stable. For the upcoming FY 2026-27, real GDP is expected to grow between 6.8% and 7.2%. This demonstrates India’s ability to maintain strong momentum even during times of global uncertainty.

The ongoing conflict in West Asia is likely to remain an important external risk for the Indian economy in the near term. India’s high dependence on imported crude oil and energy supplies from the region makes it vulnerable to supply disruptions, higher freight costs and volatility in global commodity prices. A sustained rise in crude prices may increase the import bill, widen the current account deficit and place pressure on the Indian rupee, while also adding to inflation and affecting consumer spending.

The impact may also be felt across sectors that rely heavily on fuel, imported inputs and smooth logistics, including aviation, chemicals, fertilisers, logistics and other energy-intensive industries. Prolonged instability in West Asia may also affect trade routes, remittance flows and the operating environment for exporters and import-dependent businesses. While India’s macroeconomic position remains supported by foreign exchange reserves and strategic petroleum buffers, the conflict could still weigh on growth, margins and external stability if elevated energy prices and supply chain pressures persist.

This growth will likely be driven by continued government spending on infrastructure, a steady increase in private sector investment, and a strengthening manufacturing base. Additionally, the services sector is expected to maintain its consistent expansion. Supported by a stable economy and steady policies, India is well-prepared to manage global challenges while ensuring that economic progress remains inclusive and sustainable over the long term.

(Source: PIB)

Staple Food Market

India's staple food market is undergoing a gradual shift from loose and unbranded products towards branded and packaged offerings, supported by changing consumer preferences, wider organised retail access and the expansion of digital commerce. The India staple food market was valued at $57.93 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $85.72 billion by 2031, registering a CAGR of 6.93% during 2026-31. Grains and cereals accounted for 44.71% of the market in 2025, supported by the continued importance of rice and wheat in household and institutional consumption.

The shift towards packaged staples is being supported by greater consumer preference for hygiene, consistent quality, traceability and convenience. Organised retail, e-commerce and quick commerce are further improving accessibility and assortment across categories such as rice, wheat flour, pulses, edible oils and millets. The expansion of these channels is also providing branded players with greater opportunities to increase product visibility and introduce differentiated offerings.

Product innovation is creating additional opportunities within the category, particularly through fortification, premiumisation and functional variants. Flours such as atta, maida and rice flour are seeing greater adoption of multigrain and high-protein variants, while millet-based and value-added products are gaining visibility. Pulses and legumes are expected to be the fastest-growing product category, with a projected CAGR of 7.96% through 2031, supported by increasing protein awareness and dietary diversification among urban consumers.

The industry, however, remains exposed to agricultural supply conditions and commodity price movements. Dependence on monsoon patterns can affect the availability and cost of key raw materials, while post-harvest losses and intermediary-driven procurement channels can add to supply-chain inefficiencies. These factors can create volatility in input costs and place pressure on margins for processors and branded packaged food companies.

Indian Biscuit and Confectionery Market Indian Biscuits Market

The Indian biscuits market is evolving with changing consumption patterns, rising preference for convenient snacking and increasing consumer awareness around nutrition. The market was valued at $5.0 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $8.5 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 5.70% during 2026-34. The market is supported by demand across urban and rural markets, with product innovation and wider distribution helping manufacturers cater to changing consumer preferences.

Health and nutrition are becoming important considerations in biscuit consumption. Consumers are increasingly seeking products made with whole grains and ingredients such as oats and millets, while demand is also emerging for gluten-free, sugar-free, low calorie and fortified variants. This is encouraging manufacturers to develop products positioned around fibre, digestive health, immunity and overall wellbeing, particularly among health-conscious urban consumers.

At the same time, the category is witnessing premiumisation, with consumers showing greater interest in differentiated flavours, higher-quality ingredients and indulgent products. Rising disposable incomes and changing lifestyles are supporting demand for premium biscuits and cookies, while manufacturers are introducing variants using ingredients such as dark chocolate, nuts and dried fruits to broaden the consumption occasion.

Convenience remains another important demand driver. Busy lifestyles are increasing the preference for portable and easy-to consume snacks, supporting the adoption of single-pouch, resealable and travel-friendly packs. The expansion of e-commerce is further improving access to a wider range of packaged biscuit products, while supermarkets, hypermarkets and convenience stores continue to provide important distribution channels.

The industry is consequently moving beyond traditional biscuit consumption towards a broader portfolio spanning everyday snacking, health-oriented nutrition and premium indulgence. Continued product innovation, convenient packaging and expansion across physical and online distribution channels are expected to support the growth of the Indian biscuits market.

Indian Confectionery Market

The Indian confectionery market continues to expand, supported by rising disposable incomes, urbanisation and changing consumer preferences towards indulgent and convenient products. The market was valued at ₹398.71 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach ₹618.10 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 4.99% during 2026–34. The category continues to benefit from India's strong cultural association with sweets and gifting, while modern retail and e-commerce are improving product availability across urban and semi-urban markets.

Consumer preferences are also broadening beyond traditional confectionery towards premium and differentiated offerings. Chocolate accounted for 36.5% of the market in 2025, supported by increasing preference for premium treats, gifting and new flavour combinations. Manufacturers are introducing products that combine local flavours such as cardamom, jaggery and masala chai with contemporary confectionery formats, while premium packaging and limited-edition products are supporting consumption across gifting and celebratory occasions.

Health and wellness considerations are influencing product development within the category. Growing awareness of sugar consumption is increasing demand for sugar-free, low-calorie and functional confectionery products. Manufacturers are responding through reduced-sugar formulations and the use of natural sweeteners such as stevia and jaggery, creating opportunities for products that combine indulgence with changing consumer preferences.

Affordability remains important in a price-sensitive market. Economy products represented 49.6% of the confectionery market in 2025, supported by their wide availability through traditional retail and kirana stores. Smaller pack sizes and value packs continue to help manufacturers serve consumers across income groups, particularly in rural and semi-urban markets. At the same time, the expansion of supermarkets, hypermarkets, convenience stores and online channels is improving product visibility and providing brands with additional avenues to reach consumers.

Festivals, weddings and other social occasions remain important consumption and gifting drivers. The increasing adoption of chocolates and other contemporary confectionery products alongside traditional sweets is creating additional consumption occasions, while e-commerce and quick commerce are making products more accessible, particularly during periods of heightened seasonal demand.

The industry, however, remains exposed to rising health concerns around sugar consumption, volatility in the prices of key inputs such as sugar, cocoa and palm oil, and intense competition across organised and unorganised players. Maintaining product quality and freshness across India's varied climatic conditions also requires efficient logistics and supply-chain capabilities. Going forward, product innovation, premiumisation, healthier formulations and wider distribution across modern and digital retail channels are expected to remain important to the growth of India's confectionery market.

Indian Soya Protein Market

India's soya protein market is expanding with increasing demand for plant-based protein across food and beverage, nutritional supplements and other applications. The market was valued at $570 million in 2025 and is projected to reach $795 million by 2031, registering a CAGR of 5.65% during 2026-31, compared with a historical CAGR of 5.13% during 2020-25. The market's growth is being supported by wider use of soy protein in bakery products, beverages, meal replacements, protein powders and affordable meat substitutes.

Food and beverage applications accounted for 48.63% of demand in 2025, supported by the increasing use of soy protein in plant-based foods and other protein-enriched products. Nutritional supplements are expected to be among the faster-growing applications, supported by increasing consumer interest in protein-rich diets, sports nutrition and health-oriented products. Textured soy protein is also finding wider applications in affordable meat alternatives and other food products.

The market is witnessing a gradual shift towards higher-value and application-specific soy protein products. Soy protein isolates, concentrates and textured soy protein serve different applications based on protein content, solubility, texture and functionality. Demand for higher-purity products, organic and non-GMO grades and customised formulations is expected to support value growth, while consistent flavour, solubility and quality remain important considerations for food manufacturers and nutritional product companies.

India's soy protein supply chain remains closely linked to domestic soybean production and processing capacity. India's soy-processing system has an installed crushing capacity of approximately 11.4 million tonnes. Fluctuations in soybean availability and crushing economics can, however, affect capacity utilisation and input costs, making procurement and proximity to soybean-producing regions important factors for processors.

The market also faces increasing competition from alternative protein sources, including pea, dairy and wheat proteins. Raw-material price volatility and the availability of alternative plant-based proteins can influence demand and margins, while processors need to maintain product quality and develop application-specific capabilities to differentiate their offerings.

Going forward, the continued adoption of plant-based protein, expansion of functional foods and nutritional supplements, and wider applications of textured and higher-purity soy proteins are expected to support the growth of India's soy protein market. The ability to secure soybean supplies, maintain consistent product quality and cater to evolving food and nutrition applications will remain important for participants across the value chain.

Nutraceuticals Market

India's nutraceuticals market has grown into an important part of the health and wellness sector, offering dietary supplements, functional foods, and fortified products that support immunity, digestion, energy levels, and overall well-being. Edible Oil Market

India's edible oil market forms the backbone of household cooking and food preparation across the country, including essential cooking oils such as palm, soybean, sunflower, mustard, and rice bran, which reach consumers through kirana stores, supermarkets, and modern retail outlets. This sector meets the daily cooking needs of urban families, restaurants, and food processors, while facing ongoing supply challenges due to high import dependence. Rising health awareness has shifted preferences towards healthier oils with better fatty acid profiles and fortified options.

The Indian edible oil market reached 25.33 million tonnes in 2025 and is projected to grow to 28.34 million tonnes by 2034, exhibiting a CAGR of 1.26% during 2026-2034. Domestic production covers only 40% of demand, at 9.6 million tonnes in 2025-26, leaving a shortfall of 16.7 million tonnes to be met by imports. Home consumption dominates, with a 64% market share, driven by daily cooking requirements across households nationwide.

Regional and Segment Insights

Domestic manufacturing holds 62% market share in 2025, driven by expanded refining capacity and local processing that reduce reliance on imported finished oils. North and western India lead consumption due to higher population density and food processing activity, while rural markets grow through organised distribution networks. Palm oil remains dominant, accounting for around 60% of imports from Malaysia and Indonesia, followed by soybean oil from Argentina and Brazil. (Source: imarcgroup)

Oleochemicals Market

India's oleochemicals industry is developing as demand increases for bio-based and renewable chemical ingredients across personal care, consumer goods, food processing, pharmaceuticals and industrial applications. Oleochemicals are derived from renewable feedstocks such as vegetable oils and are used in products including surfactants, specialty esters, fatty acid derivatives and glycerol-based products. Growing applications in personal care, household and industrial cleaning, pharmaceuticals and other downstream industries are supporting demand for oleochemical derivatives in India.

The Indian oleochemicals market was valued at approximately $1.2 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $2.3 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 6.84% during 2026-2034. The market encompasses products including specialty esters, fatty acid methyl esters, glycerol esters, alkoxylates and fatty amines, with applications spanning personal care and cosmetics, consumer goods, food processing, textiles, paints and inks, industrial products, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, and polymer and plastic additives.

Demand is being supported by the increasing preference for bio-based and sustainable alternatives to petrochemical-derived products, particularly in personal care, household products and industrial applications. Rising consumption of personal care and home care products, alongside greater adoption of bio-based surfactants, lubricants, and chemical intermediates, is creating additional downstream demand. The industry is also seeing investments in domestic manufacturing capacity, particularly in Gujarat and other established chemical-manufacturing hubs.

Oil Palm Plantation Market

Oil palm is an important component of India's strategy to increase domestic edible oil production and reduce dependence on imports. The crop has a high oil yield per hectare and produces both palm oil and palm kernel oil, which are used for food and industrial applications. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana account for around 98% of India's oil palm production, while cultivation is also undertaken across Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Goa and Mizoram, with oil palm programmes expanding into several North-Eastern states.

India's oil palm cultivation has expanded under the National Mission on Edible Oils–Oil Palm (NMEO-OP), which seeks to increase domestic oil palm cultivation and crude palm oil production. As of November 2025, total oil palm coverage in India stood at 6.20 lakh hectares, of which 2.50 lakh hectares were brought under the Mission. Domestic crude palm oil production increased to 3.80 lakh tonnes in 2024-25, from 1.91 lakh tonnes in 2014-15. The Mission targets 6.5 lakh hectares of oil palm plantations by 2025-26 and crude palm oil production of 28 lakh tonnes by 2029-30.

The expansion of domestic oil palm cultivation is supported by government interventions covering planting material, maintenance, intercropping and farmer price assurance. Under NMEO-OP, the Government has also introduced a viability price mechanism for fresh fruit bunches, aimed at providing greater income protection to farmers against fluctuations in international crude palm oil prices. The programme is therefore expected to support the expansion of the domestic oil palm ecosystem while improving raw material availability for processors.

Wind Power Market

India's wind power market has emerged as a critical component of the renewable energy landscape, generating clean electricity through onshore wind turbines installed in high-wind regions and contributing significantly to the national grid. This sector supports government renewable energy targets through large wind farms developed by independent power producers and utilities, serving commercial and industrial consumers as well as residential power needs. Favourable wind resources in coastal and inland states have driven steady capacity additions despite challenges from land acquisition and grid connectivity.

The Indian wind power market reached 55.3 GW in 2025 and is projected to grow to 135.8 GW by 2034, exhibiting a CAGR of 10.17% during 2025-2034. This robust expansion stems from escalating demand for renewable energy, supportive government policies, and technological improvements in turbine efficiency and hybrid wind-solar projects.

Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka lead installations, benefiting from consistent wind speeds, established infrastructure, and state-level incentives that attract developers to these regions. Onshore projects dominate the market, with utility-scale wind farms serving as the primary application for grid connected power supply. Commercial and industrial segments drive demand through long-term power purchase agreements, ensuring stable revenue streams for operators.

Company Overview Patanjali Foods Limited (referred to as ‘Patanjali’ or the Company) is a diversified consumer and food-processing company with businesses spanning FMCG, edible oils and wind turbine power generation. The Company traces its origins to 1986 and has evolved from its traditional edible oils and soya processing operations into a broader consumer platform comprising food, biscuits, textured soya protein, nutraceuticals and home & personal care. Its business model combines consumer brands and distribution capabilities with a broad manufacturing base and participation across upstream and downstream stages of the edible oils value chain.

The Company's FMCG business has become an increasingly important part of its operating profile following the acquisition of the Biscuits and Confectionery business in 2021, the Foods business in 2022 and the Home and Personal Care business in November 2024. The HPC business completed its first full year of integration in FY 2025-26 and is now part of the FMCG segment. During FY 2025-26, the Company continued to expand its FMCG portfolio through new product launches and premiumisation initiatives, including beverages and nutraceutical offerings. The FMCG segment contributed 27.60% of annual Revenue from Operations and 61.13% of EBITDA during the year.

The Company's edible oils business remains its largest operating vertical, with activities spanning edible oil refining and seed crushing, branded and bulk edible oils, and oil palm plantations, supported by downstream opportunities in derivatives and oleochemicals. In FY 2025-26, the Edible Oils segment reported revenue of ₹29,313.54 crore, representing 18.39% YoY growth, while approximately 75% of edible oil sales were from branded edible oils. The Company also continued to expand its domestic oil palm value chain, with 1,10,722 hectares under cultivation and a total allocated area of 6.63 lakh hectares as at March 31, 2026.

The oil palm business provides an upstream component to the Company's edible oils operations. As at March 31, 2026, Patanjali had established 238 Fresh Fruit Bunch (FFB) collection and Farmer Information Centres and 48 nurseries, supporting its engagement with approximately 80,579 farmers. The Company has also signed MoUs with 12 state governments and is establishing company owned seed gardens, with mills in Mizoram and Telangana in the pipeline. Management identifies the plantation business as supporting backward integration and offering a long-term, annuity oriented opportunity.

Patanjali operates a geographically distributed manufacturing network comprising 26 manufacturing locations across India. The FY 2025-26 network includes seven refinery units, seven integrated units, three seed-crushing units, three palm-crushing units, one biscuit unit, two food units and three other units. The footprint extends across locations including Kandla, Mangalore, Kakinada, Chennai, Haldia, Patalganga, Nagpur, Guna, Gadarwara, Peddapuram, Jammu, Haridwar, Newasa and Niglok, providing manufacturing capabilities across its principal businesses.

The Company's distribution architecture is omni-channel, covering ~8,000 distributors, 84 super distributors, 1,063 Mega Stores, 434 Chikitsalayas and 3,964 Arogya Kendras and Grameen Arogya Kendras, alongside e-commerce and direct-to-consumer channels. During FY 2025-26, the Company's products reached 37 countries globally, generating export revenue of ₹ 187.77 crore. This distribution infrastructure provides the Company with multiple routes to market across general trade, its proprietary retail network, digital channels and international markets.

Alongside its consumer and food businesses, Patanjali operates a wind-power generation business. The Company uses renewable power for captive requirements, with the segment contributing ₹ 33.99 crore of revenue in FY 2025-26.

Patanjali Foods continues to increase the contribution of FMCG to its overall business while maintaining the scale of its edible oil operations. The Company's FY 2025-26 strategy combines portfolio expansion, premiumisation, brand investment, distribution development, and the integration of its acquired businesses, while its manufacturing and upstream capabilities support the broader food and edible oils value chain. The Company spent approximately 2% of revenue from operations on advertising and promotion during FY 2025-26, reflecting the increased focus on brand building and consumer engagement.

Business Segments Patanjali Foods operates across three principal business segments — FMCG, Edible Oils and Wind Turbine Power Generation. The FMCG portfolio spans food, biscuits, textured soya protein, nutraceuticals and home & personal care, while the Edible Oils business covers edible oil refining and seed crushing, branded and bulk edible oils, oil palm plantations and related downstream opportunities. The Company also operates wind power assets for renewable power generation.

Opportunities and Trends

Rural consumption and wider category penetration: Rural consumption continues to be an important driver of India's FMCG market, supported by improving economic conditions, wider distribution and increasing access to branded products. Rural FMCG volumes have continued to grow faster than urban markets, while the consumption opportunity is also broadening beyond essential categories.

For Patanjali Foods, this creates an opportunity across its diverse FMCG portfolio spanning food, biscuits, nutraceuticals and home and personal care. The Company's presence across everyday consumption categories, combined with its distribution reach, provides scope to deepen penetration in existing markets and expand the consumption base across emerging markets and smaller towns.

Formalisation of food consumption and branded packaged products: The gradual shift from loose and unbranded products towards packaged and branded formats is creating a long-term opportunity across India's food and staples market. Greater emphasis on quality, consistency, convenience and product assurance is supporting the formalisation of consumption across categories.

This trend is relevant to Patanjali Foods' portfolio of atta, ghee, pulses, spices and condiments, honey and other packaged food products. The opportunity extends beyond increasing penetration of existing categories to building stronger branded propositions across a wider range of everyday food and consumption occasions.

Health, wellness and nutrition-led consumption: Health, wellness and nutrition are becoming increasingly important considerations in consumer purchase decisions. The trend is broadening the addressable market for products offering nutritional, functional or wellness-oriented benefits, while also influencing consumer choices in everyday food and personal care.

Patanjali is positioned across several of these categories through its nutraceuticals, textured soya protein, food and staples and home and personal care portfolio. This provides an opportunity to participate in evolving consumer preferences through product innovation, portfolio expansion and differentiated propositions that combine everyday consumption with health and wellness attributes.

Premiumisation with sharper value propositions: Indian consumers are increasingly balancing value consciousness with a willingness to spend on products offering superior quality, functionality or differentiated benefits. Premiumisation is also extending beyond metropolitan markets, with rural households contributing an increasing share of premium FMCG consumption.

For the Company, the opportunity lies in addressing this emerging demand across multiple price points rather than pursuing premiumisation as a standalone strategy. Its broad portfolio across food, edible oils, biscuits and confectionery and home and personal care provides scope to offer differentiated products while retaining accessibility across diverse consumer segments.

Evolution of retail and distribution channels: The continued expansion of modern trade, e-commerce and quick commerce is changing the way consumers discover, purchase and replenish FMCG products. E-commerce accounted for an increasing share of urban FMCG sales during FY 2025-26, with quick commerce emerging as a significant contributor to digital FMCG sales.

The evolution of these channels provides Patanjali with additional avenues to improve product availability, expand assortment and access new consumer cohorts. For a portfolio spanning multiple FMCG categories, a wider channel mix can complement the traditional retail network and support greater reach across consumption occasions.

Domestic value creation across the edible-oil value chain: India's dependence on imported edible oils, together with efforts to increase domestic oilseed and oil-palm production, presents a structural opportunity for greater domestic value creation across the edible-oil value chain. The opportunity extends beyond refining to include seed crushing, oil-palm cultivation and downstream value added applications.

Patanjali's presence across refining and crushing, oil-palm plantations, speciality and bakery fats, by-products and oleochemicals provides exposure to multiple stages of this value chain. The Company's integrated capabilities provide a platform to participate in the development of domestic oilseed and oil-palm ecosystems while increasing value addition across processing and downstream applications.

Renewable energy transition and the role of wind power: India's transition towards a higher share of renewable energy is creating a structural opportunity for the development and use of clean power. India crossed 50% of cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources in June 2025, ahead of its 2030 target, while wind power capacity reached 57,443 MW as at June 30, 2026. Wind based generation during FY 2025-26 was 106 billion units.

For Patanjali, its wind power generation business provides exposure to this broader transition towards renewable energy. The Company's existing wind power assets and captive renewable-energy capabilities can contribute to the use of renewable power within its operations while supporting the broader objective of reducing dependence on conventional sources of electricity. The continued development of India's renewable-energy ecosystem also provides a supportive operating environment for renewable power assets over the longer term.

Changes in commodity prices can influence procurement costs and margins, while the ability to pass on such increases may vary across categories depending on competitive intensity and consumer price sensitivity.

The Company maintains quality control processes and compliance systems across its operations, with manufacturing and product standards being monitored as part of its operating framework. The increasing formalisation of consumption also places greater emphasis on traceability, product information and consistency, making quality and compliance integral to sustaining consumer trust.

For Patanjali Foods, this exposure is particularly relevant to the Edible Oils business, where international prices, crop conditions, freight costs, currency movements and developments in major producing markets can influence the cost of raw materials. The Company's integrated operations, procurement practices and focus on operational efficiencies provide flexibility in managing these movements, while pricing actions are calibrated to market conditions and consumer affordability.

Evolving consumer preferences and shorter product cycles Consumer preferences across food, nutrition and personal care are evolving, with increasing attention to health, nutrition, ingredients, convenience, functionality and value. These changes can create opportunities for category expansion, but also increase the pace at which products and propositions need to evolve. The emergence of new brands and product formats can further intensify competition for consumer attention and shelf space.

Competitive intensity and pricing sensitivity The Indian FMCG market continues to witness competition across national, regional and emerging brands, with players competing on product availability, price, quality, innovation and consumer engagement. Increasing consumer choice and greater price sensitivity can place pressure on market share, pricing and margins, particularly in high-volume everyday-consumption categories.

Supply-chain and geopolitical uncertainties Global supply chains remain exposed to geopolitical developments, changes in trade policies, shipping disruptions, freight and insurance costs and weather-related supply shocks. Risk Management Patanjali Foods recognises that its operating environment is influenced by macroeconomic conditions, geopolitical developments, regulatory changes, technological advancements and climate related considerations. The Company’s Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework provides a structured approach to identifying, assessing, monitoring and mitigating risks across the organisation. Risk considerations are integrated into strategic planning, business decisions and operational reviews to support business continuity and protect stakeholder interests.

The framework is supported by Board-approved policies, defined accountability and established governance mechanisms. The Board of Directors, through the Risk Management Committee (RMC), oversees the Company’s risk management framework, reviews the risk profile and evaluates the adequacy of mitigation measures. Management, through the Internal Committee and business leadership teams, is responsible for implementing the framework and integrating risk considerations into day-to-day operations and strategic decision making.

Risk identification and assessment is undertaken through periodic reviews that combine qualitative judgement with quantitative analysis to evaluate the likelihood, potential impact and interdependencies of identified risks. The process draws on scenario analysis, market intelligence, stakeholder insights, data-led analysis, specialist expertise and regulatory monitoring. Material risks are prioritised within the ERM framework and addressed through appropriate

controls, mitigation plans and contingency measures, with defined monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

The Company’s financial risk management framework covers exposures arising from commodity price fluctuations, foreign currency movements and interest rate variations. These exposures are managed under Board-approved Foreign Exchange Risk Management and Commodity Price Risk Management Policies and supported by a prudent hedging framework. Foreign currency exposures relating to imports and exports are managed through forward and futures contracts, while commodity price risks are mitigated through futures contracts, sale contracts and mutually agreed supply arrangements. The Company follows a conservative treasury philosophy and restricts derivative instruments to plain vanilla products, used solely for risk mitigation and not for speculative purposes. The Value at Risk (VaR) methodology is also used to estimate potential financial exposure under normal market conditions and support risk-informed decision-making.

The Company’s key enterprise risks, their potential impact and mitigation measures are discussed in detail in the Risk Management chapter within this annual report on page 124.

Statement by director responsible for the business responsibility report, highlighting ESG related challenges, targets and achievements (listed entity has flexibility regarding the placement of this disclosure) I am pleased to present our Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) for FY 2025-26 - a year marked by strong business momentum and continued progress on our sustainability journey. Revenue grew by approximately 19% year-on-year, supported by the commencement of commercial production at our oil palm refinery in Arunachal Pradesh and a full year of operations in the home and personal care business. PFL remains steadfast in its commitment to building a more sustainable future, guided by a strong sense of environmental responsibility. As a leading company with a diverse FMCG and edible oils portfolio, we recognise the importance of responsible sourcing, efficient manufacturing, and effective management of our emissions footprint. We set short-, medium-, and long-term ESG goals and periodically review our progress to drive continuous improvement in line with our business growth. Climate and Environment: As part of our climate strategy and approach toward carbon neutrality, we continued to focus on reducing emissions, improving water-use efficiency, expanding renewable energy and fuel use, and strengthening natural carbon sinks. During the year, we generated 62,625.29 MWh of wind energy, achieved a 32% YoY increase in renewable fuel consumption, and avoided emissions equivalent to 53,254 tCO₂ through our wind projects. We also delivered a ~16% reduction in energy intensity and a ~12% reduction in Scope 1 & 2 emission intensity (per rupee of turnover, PPP-adjusted), alongside a 68% reduction in treated water discharge, year-on-year. Agriculture, Supply Chain and Import Substitution: Recognising the importance of import substitution and supply chain resilience for edible oil raw materials, we expanded our oil palm plantations to 1,10,722 hectares under drip irrigation across 12 states - a ~23% increase over the previous year — positively impacting 80,579 farmers. These efforts contributed to approximately 10.9% import substitution, reducing our dependence on imported raw materials while strengthening local livelihoods. Social Impact and Governance: On the social front, PFL is committed to achieving zero harm for employees and contractual workers, and to continuously improving our safety performance. We promote diversity, equity, and inclusion across gender, sexual orientation, ability, and other dimensions. From a governance standpoint, PFL maintains a strong focus on digital security and reported zero cybersecurity breaches during the year. Looking Ahead: We remain committed to embedding sustainability into the core of our operations and decision-making. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling and disposing at the end of life, for (a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste. Plastic Waste: We are registered under the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework and comply with applicable requirements for the responsible management of plastic waste. E-Waste: E-waste is collected and channelized through government-authorized recyclers across India, ensuring compliance with applicable regulatory requirements. Hazardous Waste: Hazardous waste is either treated in-house through Effluent Treatment Facilities (ETFs) or safely handed over to authorized waste handlers, in accordance with prescribed regulatory norms. Other Waste: We focus on minimizing waste generation through efficient material use and optimized manufacturing processes. Our waste management approach follows the five Rs-Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover, and Residual Management-to promote resource efficiency and ensure responsible disposal of residual waste.

Health and safety management system: a. Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/ No). If yes, the coverage such system? Yes. Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) Management Systems are implemented across all our operational locations. Through our comprehensive Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) Policy, we reaffirm our commitment to providing safe and healthy working conditions for all employees while promoting a proactive culture of health and safety. The policy is publicly available on our official website. Our manufacturing facilities are certified to ISO 45001, demonstrating our commitment to systematically identifying and managing occupational health and safety risks, preventing work-related injuries and ill health, and continually improving our OH&S performance. We remain committed to conducting our operations responsibly, safeguarding the well-being of our employees, protecting the environment, and contributing positively to the communities in which we operate. The Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) Policy can be accessed through the following link: https://www.patanjalifoods.com/brsr policies/. b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the entity? We have adopted a comprehensive and systematic approach to identifying work-related hazards and assessing occupational health and safety risks to maintain a safe and healthy workplace. Our safety management framework integrates periodic safety audits, workplace inspections, and Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) methodologies to proactively identify potential hazards and implement preventive controls before incidents occur. A key component of our safety culture is the near-miss reporting system, which encourages employees to report potential incidents and unsafe conditions. Reported cases are thoroughly investigated to identify root causes, implement corrective and preventive actions, and strengthen risk controls. In addition, Environmental, Health and Safety (EHS) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are implemented across all operations to ensure consistent adherence to safe work practices. Regular training programmes, safety awareness initiatives, Safety Talks, and Toolbox Talks further reinforce employees’ understanding of workplace hazards and the required control measures. Our key processes for identifying work-related hazards and assessing risks for both routine and non-routine activities include: n Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA): Conducted for routine and non-routine activities on an annual basis or whenever significant process changes occur. n Periodic Safety Audits: Undertaken to identify workplace hazards, evaluate associated risks, and monitor the effectiveness of existing control measures. n Hazard and Operability Studies (HAZOP): Performed for chemical processes to systematically identify process hazards and operational risks. n Pre-Start Safety Reviews (PSSR): Conducted before commissioning new processes, following process modifications, and prior to plant restart after preventive maintenance activities. n Online Work Permit System with Job Safety and Environmental Analysis (JSEA): Implemented to manage non-routine work safely by identifying hazards and establishing appropriate risk control measures. n Management of Change (MoC): Applied to all changes involving personnel, machinery, materials, processes, or operating conditions to ensure risks are assessed and effectively managed before implementation.

These initiatives are supported by our comprehensive Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) Policy, which is applicable across all 
operations. Through the consistent implementation of these risk management practices and continual employee engagement, we 
achieved reduction in Lost Time Injury (LTI) incidents across our Company. 
c. Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. (Y/N) 
Yes. We have established a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) framework across our business operations 
to enable workers to promptly report work-related hazards and take appropriate measures to protect themselves from potential 
risks. Key mechanisms include: 
1. Direct Reporting: Workers can report hazards and unsafe conditions directly to their supervisors or designated safety personnel. 
2. Incident Reporting: A formal incident reporting mechanism is in place to document hazards and incidents. Any deliberate 
non-reporting or concealment of incidents is subject to appropriate disciplinary action, supporting transparency and timely 
implementation of Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA). 
3. Safety Committee Meetings: Regular safety committee meetings provide a structured platform for workers to raise safety 
concerns, discuss hazards, and identify appropriate mitigation measures. 
4. Safety Observation Register: An online safety observation register enables workers to report unsafe acts and conditions, 
facilitating early intervention and preventing potential incidents. 
5. Incident Management System: Workers can report incidents through a standardized incident management system, ensuring 
consistent documentation, investigation, and follow-up. 
6. Regular Plant Rounds: Routine plant rounds and interactions with shop-floor workers provide opportunities to identify and 
address safety concerns directly at the workplace. 
7. EHS Software: An online EHS platform facilitates incident reporting and tracking across locations. Reported incidents are 
reviewed and appropriate CAPA measures are implemented, with incident learning reports shared with relevant personnel 
to prevent recurrence. 
These mechanisms promote a proactive safety culture, encourage transparent reporting, and enable workers to raise concerns 
and take appropriate action when exposed to work-related hazards, thereby supporting a safe and healthy working environment. 
d. Do the employees/ workers of the entity have access to non-occupational medical and healthcare services? (Yes/No) 
Yes, all manufacturing facilities provide access to non-occupational medical and healthcare services in accordance with the 
statutory requirements under the Factories Act, 1948. First-aid facilities are available at workplaces to address immediate medical 
needs, while employees and workers have continued access to medical treatment for non-occupational health concerns. In addition, 
all units have tie-ups with reputed hospitals to facilitate timely medical assistance during emergencies. Depending on eligibility, 
employees are also covered under Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) and medical insurance, providing coverage for both 
occupational and non-occupational healthcare needs.

Key audit matter How our audit addressed the key audit matter Revenue recognition from sale of products Refer notes 2 (I) (i) and 20 to the accompanying standalone financial statements for the material accounting policy information on revenue recognition and related financial statement disclosures. The Company derives its revenue primarily from the sale of edible oils and fast moving consumer goods to wide range of customers across various geographies. The Company recognises revenue from the sale of products in accordance with Ind AS 115, “Revenue from Contracts with Customers” (‘Ind AS 115) when the control of products being sold is transferred to the customer and there is no unfulfilled obligation. The sales contracts/arrangements with customers have distinct/varying commercial terms which requires significant management’s judgment in determining the timing of transfer of control and measurement of the transaction price net of variable consideration on account of rebates/ discount schemes. Further, the Company considers revenue as key benchmark for evaluating performance and hence, there is risk of revenue being overstated due to pressure to achieve performance targets and earning expectations and accordingly, in line with the requirements of the Standards on Auditing, revenue is determined to be an area involving significant risk which requires significant auditor attention.

Our audit procedures in relation to revenue recognition from sale of products included, but were not limited to the following:

• Obtained an understanding of the management’s process for revenue recognition and accounting for discounts and ongoing incentive schemes; 
• Assessed the appropriateness of revenue recognition policy, including those relating to discounts and incentive schemes and ensured that it is in accordance with Ind AS 115; 
• Involved our IT specialists to evaluate the design and test operating effectiveness of the Company’s internal automated controls including general IT controls, and key IT application controls implemented by the management over recognition of revenue; 
• Evaluated the design and tested the operating effectiveness of key internal financial controls over revenue recognition including those relating to determination of variable consideration and satisfaction of performance obligations; 
• Performed test of details on selected samples of revenue from sale of products recorded during the year, including specific period before and after year end by verifying the underlying supporting documents including customer contracts/ agreements, sales invoices, shipment terms, and the proof of dispatch/delivery etc. in order to ensure that correct amount of revenue is recorded in the correct period;

a Statement of Compliance 
The financial statement of the Company have been prepared in 
accordance with the Indian Accounting Standards (hereinafter
